text: (a) Πρὸς αἰτίαν τινὰ κίνησιν ἔχον. Spectat hoc præcipue ad causam quæ finis est, ad quam movetur, quod ex illa ut efficiente, est. Nec bene Picus expressit, Ad ullam prorsus causam refertur; cum referri ad causam etiam dicatur, quod ad eam ut auctorem quovis modo suam refert originem, etiamsi ad eam non moveatur; ut in divinis, Filius ad Patrem ut αἰτίαν refertur (uti Græcis loqui moris est), non tamen ad ipsum moveri seu motum habere, ut πρὸς αἰτίαν (tanquam scilicet ad finem) ulli eorum ac Catholici dicant; quod non sit propter finem, sed ipse cum Patre, et Spiritu sancto unus sit omnium finis, quod una bonitas, uti et natura: idcirco dictus Greg. Theologo atque Maximo, propter se, ἀναίτιος· nullam causam aut finem habens, qui propter nos, δι' αἰτίαν· propter causam est, qua scilicet homo factus est. Castigatius ergo in theologia loquendum, ne quid inde nedum obscuritatis, sed et erroris theologorum castigatissimo Maximo, in suis de theologia accedat.
anchorLine: νησιν ἔχον (a). Τὸ δὲ μὴ οὕτως ἔχον, οὐδὲ κυρίως ὤν,
en: The editor comments on the Greek phrase 'having a motion toward some cause': this chiefly concerns the cause that is the end toward which a thing moves, since it exists from that cause as from an efficient cause. Picus did not express it well in saying 'it is referred to no cause at all', since a thing is also said to be referred to a cause when it traces its origin to it in some way, even if it is not moved toward it; as in the Godhead the Son is referred to the Father as to the cause (as the Greeks are accustomed to say), yet he is not moved toward him, nor has motion, as toward a cause in the sense of an end, in the way Catholics speak of any of them: for he is not so for the sake of an end, but with the Father and the Holy Spirit is the one end of all, as there is one goodness, as there is one nature. Hence he is called by Gregory the Theologian and by Maximus 'without cause' (anaitios), having no cause or end, in so far as he is for himself, but 'through a cause' (di' aitian), on account of the cause, in so far as he became man for our sake. One must therefore speak with more care in theology, lest any obscurity, still less any error, creep into the theology of Maximus, the most careful of theologians.

text: (b) Ζωὴν ὑφεστῶσαν οὐσιωδῶς συνυπάρχουσαν. Deerat editis illa vox συνυπάρχουσαν, cujus absentia vere obscurum Maximi capitulum reddebat, quasi et istud participium superius positum referret; diceretur­que et Vita sic subsistens Verbum gignere, seu aliquid aliud illi præstare, cum ab illo potius accipiat; a quo et procedit, ut una cum Patre ejus principio, ut docet fides catholica. Scite vero Maximus ex discretis seu notionalibus in Deo, probat conjuncta et essentialia: Verbum scilicet mente præditum, quod a Mente essentialiter subsistente (Patre scilicet) nascendo esse habeat; idemque vivere, quod Vitæ essentialiter subsistenti, Spiritui sancto, coexsistat.
anchorLine: εστῶσαν οὐσιωδῶς συνυπάρχουσαν (b), τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ
en: On the words 'Life subsisting essentially, co-existing.' The editor reports that earlier editions lacked the word synuparchousan (co-existing), without which Maximus's chapter was truly obscure, as if that participle referred back to the participle placed above; and it might then be said that Life, so subsisting, begets the Word or does something else for him, whereas he rather receives from him, from whom Life also proceeds, together with the Father, as from one principle, as the catholic faith teaches. Maximus argues skilfully from the distinct, or notional, features in God to the joint and essential ones: the Word, endowed with mind, has his being by birth from the Mind subsisting essentially (the Father), and likewise lives because he co-exists with the Life subsisting essentially, the Holy Spirit.

text: (c) Μόνου μόνος οὐσιωδῶς ἀνάρχου Λόγου γεννήτωρ. Vox ἄναρχος Græcis dubii sensus, quod et existentiam ab æterno ante omnem durationem significet, et quod nullam ab alio originem habet. Sic optime Gregorius Theologus in suis de theologia, primique ratione, etiam ἄναρχον Filium ac Verbum catholice admittit, negatque merito ratione secundi, ut nobis constet μο[...]αρχία ac beatæ Trinitatis unitas, ipsa una relatione ad unum, non quasi sint tria non coordinata. Non bene itaque mihi Picus: Solus solius origine carentis Verbi secundum substantiam genitor; quod videtur implicare in adjecto, et negare Verbi nativitatem, [...] astruit: quis enim, quove modo genitor, cujus ge-nitura omnis expers originis sit? cum nativitas et gigni, ipsa sit origo seu processio viventis a viv[...] conjuncto, etc. Non ergo totum sic theologica tractare homini non theologo. De Spiritu sancto quod loquitur Maximus, omnium communiter Græcorum est: qui tamen caute terminum excludentem [...] apponunt processioni Verbi a parte principii, [...] μόνος Λόγου γεννήτωρ, nunquam vero processioni Spiritus sancti: ut nulla sit nostra, Græcorumque olim discordia, sed quam deinceps animorum contentio invexit, aliis impugnantibus, quod illi explicationis causa addendum sibi indulserunt.
anchorLine: σιωῶς ἀνάρχου Λόγου Γεννήτωρ (c)· καὶ μόνης
en: On the words 'sole father, in his essence, of the sole unoriginate Word.' The Greek word anarchos is ambiguous: it can mean existence from eternity before all duration, and also having no origin from another. So Gregory the Theologian in his theological works rightly allows the Son and Word to be 'without beginning' in the first sense and rightly denies it in the second, so that the monarchy and unity of the blessed Trinity stand clear. The editor therefore finds Picus's gloss, 'sole begetter of the Word who has no origin, according to substance', poor: it seems self-contradictory and to deny the Word's birth, which Picus himself asserts; for who, and how, is a begetter whose begetting is wholly without origin, since birth and being begotten are themselves the origin or procession of a living thing from a living thing joined to it? One should not treat theology so loosely, if one is no theologian. As for what Maximus says of the Holy Spirit, it is common to all the Greeks, who nevertheless take care to add the exclusive term 'only' to the procession of the Word from the principle, never to the procession of the Spirit, so that there is no discord of ours; the long-standing Greek discord, which later strife of minds introduced, arose when others objected to what the Greeks allowed themselves to add for explanation. (Some line-ends in this note are inked over and are marked [...].)

text: (d) Καὶ ἔτι μᾶλλον τῆς καθ' ὑπερουσιότητα θέσεως, ἀπείρως ἐξηρημένος. Significant hæc divinam eminentiam, separatione ac singularitate supra res omnes, omnemque earum positionem, seu affirmantem conceptum. Id enim illud ἐξηρημένως, qua voce in hunc sensum sæpius utitur Dionysius. Eminet ergo infinite, ab omnique secretus superessentiali positione; omni scilicet affirmatione nostra de superessentiali essentia ac natura. Paulo rudius Picus: Imo potius a thesi substantiam excedenti distat infinite.
anchorLine: ὑπερουσιότητα θέσεως, ἀπείρως ἐξηρημένος (d)· ὁ
en: On the Greek words 'and still more than the positing in the manner of super-essentiality, infinitely removed.' These words signify the divine eminence, set apart and singular above all things and above every positing of them, that is, every affirmative concept. For that is what the word exeremenos means, which Dionysius often uses in this sense. So God is infinitely eminent and set apart from every super-essential positing, namely from all our affirmation about the super-essential essence and nature. Picus, a little more crudely: 'Rather, he is infinitely distant from a positing that surpasses substance.' (Legibility note: the second instance of the Greek participle is blurred; read as ἐξηρημένως.)

text: (f) Ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων. Quod paulo ante legerat Picus, ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων, fallentibus oculis ac præcurrente calamo, hic legit ac reddidit, pro hominibus; etsi illius Græca perinde habeant ὑπὲρ ἄνθρωπον, supra hominem: quod unum aptum est. Est enim ratio cur ignotum et abstrusum semperque myste-rium incarnationis mysterium; quod scilicet div[...] altiorisque ordinis est, non pro humana ratione.
anchorLine: διὰ παντὸς ἔχων ἀνέκφαντον· ὑπὲρ ἄνθρωπον (f) γὰρ
en: On 'huper anthropon'. The editor says that Picus, who a little before had read 'huper anthropon' (for men), with deceived eyes and a hurrying pen, here read and rendered 'for men', although the Greek of the passage, in both places alike, has 'huper anthropon' (above man, beyond man): that alone fits. For there is a reason why the mystery of the incarnation is always unknown and hidden: that it is divine and of a higher order, not for human reason. (The last word of one line is inked over and marked [...].)

text: (g) Ἡ τῶν ἁγίων δυσπάθεια. Sensus Maximi est, ea pugna vitii ac virtutis, quasi durari qui serio virtutis cultores sint, ut non facile lædi a vitio possint. Hæc enim vis ejus vocis, ut hic Maximo usurpatur, cujus significationis exstant exempla apud Bud. et Henr. Stephan. Nihil ad rem quod reddit Picus, Repugnantia affectuum quæ est in sanctis: quem sensum vox illa non partitur. Posset quidem reddi, Molestia, labor, etc., ut cap. 19 et 21; sed minus quadrat pro Maximi hic instituto. Quod in fine cap. est, Τῆς δὲ, ὅπως κατάσχῃ τοὺς ἀγαθοὺς, κἂν ταῖς συμφοραῖς τὸ πλέον ἔχοντας, misere depravat idem Picus, dum ita reddit: Hæc autem, ut bonos et locupletiores in calamitatibus contineat. Plene vult Maximus, continere virtutem in officio probos, quorum etiam in ærumnis partes potiores sunt: Melior longe conditio quam malorum. Dicamus nos, Qui ont l'avantage même dans les afflictions, etc. Hæc nimirum evangelica promissio: Centies tantum nunc in tempore hoc, cum persecutionibus, Marc. x, 30; quod egregie Maximus dicit, κατορθοῦντας κολάζεσθαι, idcirco puniri malisque affici, quod virtutem colamus, et officii tenaces simus. Id certe qui præstent, inque illis patientiam teneant, seu etiam gaudeant, virtute adulti ac Christiana fortitudine, omnium vere beatissimi, adversumque omnes τὸ πλέον ἔχοντες. Rem Maximus magis explicat sequenti cap. cujus in fine aurea sententia est, Ῥῶσις ψυχῆς τοῖς ὑπομένουσιν, ὁ τοῦ σώματος αἰκισμός: Robur animi per patientiam, injuria ac sugillatio corporis.
anchorLine: δυσπάθεια (g) · τοῦ μὲν, ὅπως κρατήσῃ φιλονει-
en: On 'the impassibility (dyspatheia) of the saints.' The editor explains that Maximus means that, in the struggle of vice and virtue, those who are earnestly devoted to virtue are as if hardened, so that they cannot easily be harmed by vice; this is the force of the word as Maximus uses it here, and examples of that sense are found in Budaeus and Henri Estienne. What Picus gives, 'the conflict of the affections that is in the saints', is beside the point, since the word does not bear that sense; it could be rendered 'trouble, toil' (as in chapters 19 and 21), but that suits Maximus's purpose here less well. The editor also says Picus wrongly renders the final clause of the chapter ('that he may hold the good, even in misfortunes having the advantage'), as if it meant 'that he may keep the good and the richer in calamities'; Maximus fully intends to keep the upright in their duty, whose lot even in hardships is the better one, or who rejoice, grown strong in virtue and Christian fortitude, the most blessed of all and having the advantage over all adversaries. The editor suggests the gospel promise (a hundredfold 'now in this time, with persecutions', Mark x, 30), which Maximus states well in saying that those who do right are punished and afflicted because they cultivate virtue and hold to duty; and Maximus explains the matter further in the next chapter, whose last line is a golden saying: 'strength of soul for those who endure: the scourging of the body.' (This quoted saying is rendered in the note itself as 'robur animi per patientiam, injuria ac sugillatio corporis'.) The note also includes a French phrase, 'Qui ont l'avantage même dans les afflictions', cited from a translation.

text: (h) Καὶ ἀδιάπτωτος. Quasi ipsa in se constans et firma, et quod ait Apost. I, Cor. xiii, 8 : ἡ ἀγάπη οὐδέποτε ἐκπίπτει. Charitas nunquam excidit : ea nimirum ratione, qua reliquarum virtutum theologicarum complementum est; τὸ ἔσχατον ὀρεκτὸν ὅλον ὅλῃ περιπτυσσομένῃ, totum tota complectens supremum appetibile, ejusque præsentis fruitione, fidei ac spei in ipsum motus quiete sistens. Quæ sic clara ac theologica, quis ferat ita Pico, nulla sensu reddite, Quæ post omnia, prorsus expetenda est et tota induenda ?
anchorLine: ἀδιά- πτωτος (h) καὶ μένουσα.
en: On 'and unfailing.' The editor explains it as 'in itself constant and firm,' and as the Apostle says in 1 Cor. xiii, 8, 'love never fails': that is, charity is the completion of the other theological virtues, the last object of desire, wholly embracing the whole, the supreme desirable, and bringing the motion of faith and hope toward it to rest in the enjoyment of it as present. Such clear and theological language, he says, Picus renders without any sense: 'which after all things is to be wholly sought and wholly put on.' The note is a comment on the text and neither supplies nor deletes a word.

text: (i) Διὰ τὴν μίαν καὶ ἀπαράλλακτον... βούλησιν. Picus quod eam vocem ἀπαράλλακτον, immutabilem, reddit; statimque post c. 29, in illis verbis, τὴν τοῦ θεουμένου πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν κατὰ τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἀπαραλλαξίαν, Deificati a Deo impossibilem separationem ; longe a vero est, sanaque doctrina. Utrobique enim τὸ ἀπαράλλακτον et ἀπαραλλαξία, exacta similitudo est, nulla quasi differentia et evariatione : Hesych. [...] Quod reddere voluerit Philox. et vetus Gloss. Steph. cum indiscretum exponunt, Greg. in diem Christi Natal. ἡ ἀπαράλλακτος εἰκών : Imago per omnia similis. Nihilque theologis crebrius, ea vocis illius acceptione, vel in divinis personis, vel in quibus perfecta secundum bonitatem, quanta homini concessa, cum Deo similitudo est per charitatem quæ tamen nec statum immutabilem, nec impossibilem a Deo separationem facit, extra ipsam consummationem et Dei visionem, de qua Maximus hic non agit. Fraudem fecerit Pico Steph. in Thesauri indice, ubi nullo auctore (nescio an ex veteri aliquo glossario, vel ex suo capite) ἀπαραλλαξία : Non mutari, seu immutabilitas, constantia ; cum tamen idem, t. I, bene exponat ; arguatque Bilibal. in loco allato Greg. quasi perperam reddiderit, incommutabilis similitudo.
anchorLine: λαχτον ἀμφοτέρων κατὰ τὸ θέλημα βούλησιν (i) τε
en: On 'through the one and unchanging will.' The editor objects that Picus renders the Greek word 'aparallakton' as 'unchangeable', and soon after, in chapter 29, in the phrase 'the deified man's aparallaxia towards God in respect of the good', as 'the impossible separation of the deified from God'; this is far from the truth and from sound doctrine. In both places 'aparallakton' and 'aparallaxia' mean exact likeness, with almost no difference or variation (Hesychius). The editor says what Philoxenus and the old Glossary of Estienne meant, when they explain it as 'indiscrete', and quotes Gregory (Christmas oration), 'the image in all things alike'. Theologians use this sense constantly, whether of the divine persons or of those in whom, so far as is granted to man, likeness to God is perfect by charity, which yet makes neither an unchangeable state nor an impossible separation from God, setting aside the final consummation and the vision of God, which Maximus is not discussing here. Picus may have been misled by Estienne's Thesaurus index, where, without naming an author, the word is glossed 'not to change, or immutability, constancy', although the same work (vol. 1) explains it well; and Bilibaldus is said to argue, on the Gregory passage, that it was wrongly rendered 'unchangeable likeness'. (One Greek citation in the right-column continuation of this note, from Hesychius, is garbled in the scan and marked [...].)

text: (j) Ὡς ἀληθῶς. Legendum potius videatur, ὡς ἀγαθῶς. Divina enim bonitas una ratio est, cur Deus sic natura unitos, voluerit animorum consensu ac voluntatibus uniri; præceperitque misereri, ac miserendo, impetrandæ a Deo misericordiæ aptari. τὸν ὡς ἀληθῶς, nihil hic valde aptum, aut necessarium.
anchorLine: ὡς ἀληθῶς (j) ὠθῶν τὸ ἀνθρώπινον, τὰς σωτηρίους
en: On 'truly.' The editor suggests that one should rather read 'as to the good' (hos agathos), for the divine goodness is the one reason why God, having so united us in nature, wished us to be united also in minds and wills, and commanded us to have mercy, and by showing mercy to be fitted to obtain mercy from God. The phrase 'truly' is, he says, of no great aptness or necessity here. This is a conjecture: the editor would read 'hos agathos' in place of 'hos alethos'.
note: The note's second occurrence of the Greek, 'τὸν ὡς ἀληθῶς', is printed so in the foot; the first line's 'ὡς ἀγαθῶς' is the conjecture.

text: (k) Ἀναλγησίαν εἰσηγησαμένη. Quasi indolentiam, immisericordis animi duritiem, stoliditatem, stuporem. Vocant Græci et ἀπάθειαν : non laudabilem illam, quæ est coercitis ratione affectibus, et cui tantopere student Christiani philosophi, ipsique olim ethnici, sed quam vituperat Paulus Rom. i ; dum malorum exemplo ponit ἀστόργους, Vulg. sine affectione. Nullo scilicet naturalis amoris ac pietalis sensu præditos : quæ est affectuum absentia, quales exigit ratio, ipsaque sibi una condita rationalis natura. Non satis apte Picus insensibilitate introducta : cum sensilis vox magis passive accipiatur, pro eo quod sensu attingi potest, seu quod eum movet. Nec longe felicius, quod sequitur, αὐτὴν καθ᾽ ἑαυτῆς τὴν φύσιν διὰ τῆς γνώμης ἐξώπλισε. Ipsam in sese naturam ingenii solertia armavit. Aliud certe γνώμη, qua sic scissa natura, quam ingenii solertia. Ipsa nimirum sui juris voluntas ac libera, eoque discors in singulis, quorum est γνωμική, voluntas trahensque naturam in diversa ac in ea faciens inæqualitatem.
anchorLine: αὐτῆς ἀναλγησίαν εἰσηγησαμέ- νη (k), αὐτὴν καθ᾽ ἑαυτῆς τὴν φύσιν
en: On 'having introduced insensibility.' The editor takes it to mean indolence: the hardness, stolidity, torpor of a merciless mind. The Greeks also call it 'apatheia', but not the praiseworthy kind, in which the passions are restrained by reason, which Christian philosophers (and the pagans of old) so strive for, but the kind Paul condemns in Romans i, where he names the 'astorgous' (Vulgate 'without affection'), those with no feeling of natural love and piety. Picus's 'insensibilitate introducta' is not quite apt, since 'sensilis' is taken more passively (what can be perceived by sense, or moves it). Nor is it much happier in the next phrase, 'armed nature against itself by the gnome': the editor says 'gnome' is something other than ingenuity: it is the will, free and so discordant in individuals, which draws nature into opposite directions and makes inequality in it.

text: l) Πάσης παθῶν ἐπινοίας. Pro λογισμοῦ videtur usurpasse; ut significet ipsum vitium et affectum animo hærentem juxta quod Varin. ἐπίνοια, ὅταν τις τὰ ὄντα ἐν τῇ διανοίᾳ θεωρῇ. Non satis bene Picus : Ab omni affectuum opinione. Possit et subtilem cogitatum et adinventionem sonare, uti sequenti statim cap. Τὰς ἀμυθήτους τῶν φθοροποιῶν παθῶν ἐπινοοῦμεν γενέσεις. Ut velit fore liberos omni vitio ac affectu, tum cujus nobis ipsi auctores simus, propria adinventione, tum cujus dæmones sua suggestione.
anchorLine: πάσης παθῶν ἐπινοίας (l) καὶ δαιμονιώδους κακουργίας πάντως
en: On 'of every contrivance of passions.' The editor thinks the word is used in place of 'reasoning' (logismos), meaning the vice itself and the affection lodged in the mind, as Varinus gives 'epinoia: when one contemplates things that are in the mind'. Picus's 'from every opinion of the passions' is not quite right. The word may also mean a subtle thought and invention, as in the next chapter, 'we conceive the unspeakable generations of the destructive passions': so that he wishes us free of all vice and passion, both that of which we ourselves are the authors by our own invention, and that of which the demons are authors by their suggestion.

text: (m) Μὴ τὸ σῶμα περιποιούμενος. Ubique in nimium corporis amorem, illiusque curam non ex ratione (quæ illa vitiosa φιλαυτία est) refert Maximus vitia reliqua; et hic, quod quis creaturæ serviat. Male rem Picus exprimit, Creaturæ inservire nequit, nisi præparato prius corpore. In reliquis etiam laborat Picus, nec altos Maximi sensus assequi satis potest, aut reddere.
anchorLine: οὕτως οὔτε τῇ κτίσει λατρεύειν, μὴ τὸ σῶμα περιποι- ούμενος (m)· καθ' ὃ σῶμα τὴν φθοροποιὸν ἐπιτελῶν
en: On 'not caring for the body.' The editor says that Maximus everywhere traces the remaining vices to an excessive love of the body and the care of it that does not come from reason (which is that vicious self-love, philautia); and here, that one serves the creature. Picus expresses the matter badly, 'he cannot serve the creature unless the body has first been prepared'. In the rest too Picus struggles, and cannot adequately grasp or render Maximus's deep meanings.

text: (n) Κατὰ τὸν θεῖον Ἀπόστολον, καὶ τοὺς ἀμφ᾽ αὐτόν. Et hic longe aberrat, dum ita reddit, Ex sententia divini Apostoli et ex ejus præcepto. Cum sit, Divini Apostoli et similium more, velut divinus Apostolus (cujus nedum hæc sunt verba, verum etiam de ipso et in sua persona dicta) virique cum illo apostolici ac divi quibus sic Christus vita sit. Piget sic ex trivio res adnotare; sed in vitium vitiie cogor alieno.
anchorLine: τοὺς ἀμφ᾽ αὐτὸν (n), τοὺς ζῶντας μὲν οὐδαμῶς ἰδίαν
en: On 'according to the divine Apostle, and those about him.' The editor says Picus again goes far astray in rendering it 'by the opinion of the divine Apostle and by his precept'. The sense is 'in the manner of the divine Apostle and of those like him', the divine Apostle (whose words these are, and are spoken of himself and in his own person) and the apostolic and holy men for whom Christ is thus their life. He is ashamed to annotate things in this plebeian way, but is forced to by another's fault.

text: (o) Ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ δεικνὺς γνώριμον τὴν ψυχήν. Et hoc tam clarum, ita Picus : Ex seipso declarat præclaram quidem esse animam. Hæcne vis, τοῦ ἀκαθάρτου καὶ ἐσπιλωμένου χιτῶνος· immundi illius et conspurcati involucri ac pallii, declarare esse præclaram animam ? Nugæ. Manifestat eam, seu reddit manifestam ex seipso ; sic nempe factam immundam ac inquinatam ; quæ sibi pro divina turpem illam formam imaginemque indiderit. Magni ubique cum pari pietate sensus Maximi.
anchorLine: ἑαυτοῦ δεικνὺς γνώριμον τὴν ψυχὴν (ο), μορφὴν ἄλλην
en: On 'showing the soul to be known from itself.' The editor quotes Picus's rendering, 'from himself he declares the soul to be indeed excellent', and asks whether the force of 'the unclean and defiled tunic' (the unclean and befouled garment) is to declare the soul excellent: nonsense. It makes the soul manifest, or renders it manifest from itself, made unclean and defiled, which has put on itself that base form and image instead of the divine. Maximus's meanings are great everywhere, as is his piety.

text: (p) Τῶν γεγονότων τὴν ἄπταιστον γνῶσιν. Quasi absque ullo errore, in qua non sit impingere et labi. Utitur sæpe Maximus pro certa jam perfectaque scientia, non morum, sed speculabilium ; uti hic etiam. Id enim τῶν γεγονότων γνῶσις · Scientia rerum a Deo conditarum ; cujus perfectio ipsa veritas et certitudo. Non bene itaque Picus, immaculatam reddit : forte Hesych. fretus , cui ἀπταίστως, ἀκαταγνώστως est, refertque Varin. verum id cum de morum offensa sermo sit. Suid. adductam vocem non exposuit, quod ex simplicis ipsa ratione, pro subjecta materia exponenda sit.
anchorLine: βάλλων, τῶν γεγονότων τὴν ἄπταιστον συλλέγεται γνῶσιν (p).
en: On 'the faultless knowledge of created things.' The editor glosses it as 'without any error, in which there is no stumbling or slipping.' Maximus often uses it for knowledge already certain and perfect, not of morals but of things contemplated, as here: it is the knowledge of created things, the knowledge of things made by God, whose perfection is truth itself and certainty. Picus is therefore wrong to render it 'immaculate', perhaps trusting Hesychius, for whom 'aptaistos' is 'akatagnostos' (as Varinus reports); but that applies when the talk is of offence in morals. Suidas did not explain the word as quoted, because it must be explained from the simple sense, according to the subject-matter in hand.

text: (q) Εἰς τὸν ὅρον συνετέλουν τῆς φύσεως. Quasi contribuerentur, et quod vulgatius clariusque reddidi, spectarent, pertinerent ad naturæ definitionem. Nihil bene Picus : Etenim ad finem quoque contulissent. Aliud ὅρος, alius finis : etsi ὅρος quoque terminus dicitur, qui ipsa definitio est. Etiam τὸ [continues on p-0616]
anchorLine: ἂν συνετέλουν τῆς φύσεως (q). Λέγω δὴ παρὰ τοῦ
en: On 'they would contribute to the definition of nature.' The editor takes it as 'would be contributed', and as he has rendered more commonly and plainly, 'would look to, would belong to, the definition of nature.' Picus's 'for they would also have contributed to the end' is not good: horos (definition) is one thing, end another, although horos also means a boundary, which is the definition itself. The note breaks off at 'Etiam to' and continues at the head of the foot block on the next page.

text: προηγουμένως : non bene ab initio : est, primo seu primario; prima scilicet destinatione, ac quasi Deus creando hominem, his illum stipare intenderit. Negat Maximus cum Nysseno ; ac verum omnino de affectibus ut sunt vere πάθη seu perturbationes, vitiumque olent, nec perfecte subjiciuntur rationi. Alioqui certe etiam ipsi ad hominis definitionem spectant, non quidem sub formali ratione hominis, sed ut etiam animal exsistit ; nec enim homo purus animus ac mens est, ni Origeniane sentire velimus. Passimque Maximus aliique Patres horum ἐνέργειαν in Christo necessariam contendunt, ut veritas in eo naturæ humanæ monstraretur. Sicut ergo erant in Adamo et Eva, quibus nos nudis erubescimus, ipsa nuda, et non erubescebant, quia in eis nullum rebellantem motum sentiebant ; inque eum modum eorum corpora etiam προηγουμένως condita fuerant : sic et πάθη, affectus virium sentientium et ἐνέργειαι, prout quæque propensa erat suum finem et objectum ; sed cum summa tranquillitate, nullaque perturbatione aut molestia.
anchorLine: (see p-0615: ἂν συνετέλουν τῆς φύσεως (q))
en: Continuation of note (q) from the previous page, here on 'proegoumenos'. The editor says 'ab initio' (from the beginning) is not a good rendering; it means 'first, or primarily', that is, by first destination, as if God in creating man had intended to equip him with these. Maximus, with Nyssa, denies it; it is quite true of the affections as they are truly 'pathe', or perturbations, which smack of vice and are not perfectly subject to reason. Yet they do belong to the definition of man, not under the formal aspect of man but as he also exists as an animal; for man is not pure soul and mind, unless we wish to think as Origen did. Maximus and other Fathers everywhere maintain that these energies were necessary in Christ, so that the truth of human nature might be shown in him. Just as Adam and Eve, before whom we blush when naked, were naked and did not blush, because they felt no rebellious motion in themselves; and thus their bodies too had been made 'proegoumenos'; so also the passions, the affections of the sentient powers, and the energies, each in proportion as it was disposed toward its end and object, but with the greatest tranquillity and without disturbance or trouble.

Hæc tam clara, de timore illo incipientium, qui originem actus ex peccato, castus non sit, et qui non semper maneat, sed una cum peccato aboleatur per pœnitentiam (charitate scilicet perfecta cum foras mittente), non ferendo errore Picus, adversante Scriptura omnique theologia, Nec unquam delebitur cum peccato per pœnitentiam.
anchorLine: ζόμενος (r). Ὁ δὲ δίχα τῆς ἐπὶ πλημμελήμασι λύπης
en: On 'nor will it be forever, vanishing together with sin through repentance.' The editor says these words are quite clear, about that fear of beginners which derives its origin from sin, is not chaste, and does not last for ever but is abolished together with sin through repentance (perfect charity, namely, casting it out). Picus's rendering, 'nor will it ever be blotted out with sin through repentance', is an intolerable error, contrary to Scripture and all theology.

text: (s) Ἡ φυσικὴ πρὸς ἀρετῶν ἐνέργειαν δύναμις. Sic Maximus, hoc quod est agere definit, Naturalis facultas operandi, seu præstandi virtutes. Ac ubique τὸ φύσει opponit τῷ, παρὰ φύσιν. Sic loqui docuit Paulus, Rom. ii. Ὅταν ἔθνη φύσει τὰ τοῦ νόμου ποιῇ · quasi ex ductu atque instinctu naturæ, illique consentance ; tunc etiam cum gratia excitamur, extra quam in natura corrupta, non φύσει agimus, sed παρὰ φύσιν · etsi Maximus nihil hic peculiarius de gratia explicat, sine qua certum est nos non dignos effici beata illa passione, quæ est θέωσις, perfectaque cum Deo similitudo ejusque adeptio, omnino excedens vim et facultatem naturæ (etiam quoad modum) omni proprio actu in ea cessante, Deo sibi penitus animum subjiciente beato illo silentio, ejusque fruendi felici necessitate.
en: On 'the natural power toward the energy of the virtues.' The editor says Maximus defines 'to act' thus: the natural capacity of operating, or of achieving virtues. Everywhere he opposes 'by nature' (physei) to 'contrary to nature' (para physin), as Paul taught in Rom. ii ('when the Gentiles do by nature the things of the law'), as it were from the lead and instinct of nature, in agreement with it. Even when we are stirred by grace, apart from which, in corrupted nature, we do not act by nature but contrary to nature; although Maximus says nothing more particular here about grace, without which it is certain that we are not made worthy of that blessed passion which is deification (theosis), the perfect likeness to God and its attainment, wholly surpassing the power and capacity of nature (even as to mode), with every proper act in nature ceasing, God wholly subjecting the soul to himself in that blessed silence and in the happy necessity of enjoying him.

text: (t) Τῶν ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων τοὺς λόγους περάσαντες. Rerum, quæ ex nihilo sunt, rationibus superatis. Quod sæpius τῶν ὄντων, Maximus et alii dicunt ; certe ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων, ubi præsertim τῷ ὄντι absolute opponuntur. Sic clara, male Picus , Patimur cum sermones de his quæ non sunt, haberi solent, plene transgressi ; quibus nec mica sensus. Parique fere ἀστοχασίᾳ illi redditum, quod alto adeo sensu Maximus de eadem in patria deificatione, ἐκεῖνο γινόμενοι, ὅπερ τῆς κατὰ φύσιν δυνάμεως, οὐδαμῶς ὑπάρχει κατόρθωμα. Hoc præclarum facultatis naturalis facinus assecuti, quod nusquam subsistit. Egregium certe facinus illud, quod est nihil. Nempe patimur : qui illud efficiamur (ipsum scilicet quod patimur, quod est Deus, ipsi dii deificatione facti ) quod naturalis facultatis haud quam facinus, seu opus, exsistit (nempe beata illa passione hoc fieri), sed singularissimi divini muneris, Deique sic sibi creaturam subjicientis, cui condendo suam impressit imaginem, intelligendique ac arbitrii facultate sibi fecit affinem.
anchorLine: οὐκ ὄντων τοὺς λόγους τελείως περάσαντες (t), εἰς
en: On 'having completely passed beyond the reasons of things that are from nothing.' The editor renders it 'the reasons of things that come from nothing having been surpassed'; Maximus often says 'of things that are', but 'from not-being' certainly where it is opposed absolutely to 'that which is'. Picus renders it badly: 'We suffer, when we have wholly gone beyond the discourses which are customarily held about things that are not', where there is not a grain of sense; and he gives a similarly mistaken rendering of Maximus's lofty teaching about deification in the homeland, 'becoming that which in no way exists as a right act of natural power'. The editor takes it thus: having attained that splendid deed of natural faculty which subsists nowhere, a fine deed indeed, which is nothing. Rather, what we undergo is that to which we are made, namely God, being made gods by deification, and this is by no means a deed or work of natural faculty (since it comes by that blessed passion) but of the most singular divine gift, God thus subjecting creation to himself, impressing his own image on it in creating it, and making it akin to himself by the faculty of understanding and free choice.

text: (v) Τοὺς λόγους αὐτῶν ἀναζητῶν, ὡς νοητῶν τύπους · Eorum mente exquirit rationes, ut intellectibilium formas. Ex sensilibus enim, sic spiritaliter lectis eorum rationibus, assurgimus ad νοητὰ, res spiritales et quæ sola mente intelliguntur. Hæc Picus prorsus ἀφιλοσόφως. Sed qua de his dicuntur, ut intellectualium typis. Intellectualium νοερῶν est, sive mentium, νοητῶν, eorum quæ ab illis intelliguntur, ac velut eorum cibus sunt, uti exponit Dionys. Sic tamen passim interpretes confundunt : superiora vero, nemo ita reddat ut Picus, qui nec errorem seq. cap. mutavit.
anchorLine: ἀναζητῶν, ὡς νοητῶν τύπους (υ) ἢ λόγους αἰσθητῶν
en: On 'seeking out their reasons as types of intelligibles.' The editor glosses: he seeks out their reasons by the mind, as the forms of the intelligible. For from sensible things, their reasons having been read spiritually, we rise to the 'noeta', spiritual things and what are understood by mind alone. Picus renders this quite unphilosophically. But what is said of these is 'as to types of the intellectual (noeron)', that is, of minds; 'noeta' are what are understood by them, and are as it were their food, as Dionysius explains. Translators commonly confuse the two; and nobody should render the foregoing as Picus does, who did not even change his error in the following chapter.

text: cant, θλῖψις, ἀνάγκη, μέριμνα · quod et sæpius redditur illa vox, Afflictio, necessitas, ærumna, afflictus rerum casus. Hæc enim sunt, quæ illum efficiunt calicem, qui non nostra voluntate assumitur, sed exterius Deo auctore, vel saltem, eo permittente, adhibetur : quem ipsum tamen oblatum sponte acceptare debemus, inque eum modum, τὴν περιστατικὴν φύσεως θάνατον ὑπέρχεσθαι : mortem scilicet, qua sic malis atque ærumnis naturæ vita exstinguatur, Dei desiderio obire.
anchorLine: (call on p-0623: ἀκουσίων πειρασμῶν (x))
en: Continuation of note (x) from the previous page: 'peristasis' means what Hesychius, Varinus and others explain as 'thlipsis, anagke, merimna' (affliction, necessity, care), a word often rendered 'affliction, necessity, trouble, the stress of circumstance'. These are the things that make up the cup, which is taken not by our will but is applied from outside by God as author, or at least by his permission; we ought nevertheless to accept it willingly when offered, and in that way to undergo the 'circumstantial death of nature': the death, namely, by which the life of nature is extinguished by such evils and troubles, to die by desire of God.

text: (y) Ἀλήθειαν εἶναι λέγει. Non uno loco sic loquitur Maximus, ac si non ejus essent, quæ adhibet quasi scholia, ubi quid obscurius locutus est, ut quod hic exponit præcedens caput. Eo autem collineare videtur, ut divina scientia, ipsa potius a Deo speranda sit ac expetenda, ad quam non sufficere nostros ac virtutis labores existimemus ; aut unquam nos comprehendisse ; quod sentire, quandiu in via sumus, οἰήσεως est, toties Maximo exagitatæ ; sui opinionis ac jactantiæ ; animi sibi placentis atque superbi.
anchorLine: βʹ. Ἀλήθειαν μὲν εἶναι λέγει, (y) τὴν θείαν γνῶσιν
en: On 'he says that truth is ...'. The editor says Maximus often speaks as if what he adds as scholia were not his own, where he has said something obscurely, as what this chapter explains from the preceding one. He seems to aim at this: that divine knowledge is rather to be hoped and sought from God, and that we should not think our own labours of virtue enough for it, nor that we have ever grasped it; to think so, while we are on the way, is 'oiesis' (self-conceit), which Maximus so often attacks: a mind pleased with itself and proud.

text: (z) Κατὰ τὴν αἴσθησιν ἐνεργούμενος. Exponit ipse Maximus eam vocem active, per hoc quod dicit : κατὰ τὴν αἴσθησιν, κατὰ τὸν νοῦν κέκτηται τὴν ἐνέργειαν ; sicque optime intelligitur quod de charitate Galat. v. Δι' ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένη · Per charitatem operans, ut non male Erasm. nihil dissentanee Vulg. quæ per charitatem operatur : quem nec ita barbare locutum existimandum, ut passiva significatione eam vocem acceperit, quidquid velit videatur Hier. Ipsa sane fides est, cui operatio utaque ascribitur, etsi illi necessaria ad perfectionem omnes charitas seu dilectio, sine qua vana et atque mortua, non valens scilicet vera vitæ opera edere, nisi forte inchoatione ac disponendo ad perfectam justitiam ex motione gratiæ.
anchorLine: ἐνεργούμενος (z) · ὁ δὲ τοῦ πνεύματος κατὰ νοῦν ἐνεργούμενος
en: On 'being worked upon according to sense.' The editor says Maximus himself explains the word as active, by saying 'according to sense, according to mind he has the energy'; and so the phrase is best understood as that of Galatians v, 'faith working through love' (Erasmus rendered it well 'per charitatem operans', not at odds with the Vulgate 'quae per caritatem operatur'), which should not be thought so barbarous as to take the word in a passive sense, whatever Jerome seems to wish. Faith itself is what the operation is ascribed to, though charity or love is necessary to its perfection; without it faith is vain and dead, unable to produce true works of life, unless perhaps by beginning and by preparing for perfect justice from the motion of grace.

text: (a) Τὴν τοῦ νοεῖν καὶ νοεῖσθαι παντελῶς δύναμιν ἔχει σχολάζουσαν. Vacantem, otiantem (uti jam ὑπὲρ νόησιν, mentis cogitatu superior) habet vim animi, qua se, vel aliud quidvis cogitet aut intelligat ; divinum potius patiens illapsum, quo jam deus fiat atque exsistat. Hic planus Maximi sensus, innumeris illi locis expressus, cunctisque mysticis familiarissimus. Hoc nempe quod ait, ὑπεράνω τῆς οὐσίας τῶν ὄντων, γενόμενον, τὴν τῆς θείας καὶ ἀμάχου μονάδος δέχεσθαι φωτισμὸν, ut cap. 95 præcedentis Centenarii. Picus contrario sensu, Totis viribus in id incumbit ut intelligat et intelligatur ; quod esset ἀσχολάζουσαν, prorsusque abhorret. Verum non satis Pici provecta mens pro mysticorum silentio illo atque otio ac caligine, cui multum sit ut incumbat φυσικῇ θεωρίᾳ, non in Deum vere spiritalis excedat. Quod Maximus hic et cap. 11 τὸ διακριθῇ exponit divisus fuerit, longe est a communi explicatione. Vulg. enim, Erasm. et alii, καὶ μὴ διακριθῇ, Et non dubitaverit : quod ut ita redderent, suasit quod sequitur, ἀλλὰ πιστεύσῃ, quæ est fides miraculorum, cui opponitur hæsitatio illa et diffidentia. Hinc Suid. διακρίνεται, ἀμφιβάλλει, ἀπιστεῖ. Prior significatio magis arrisit Maximo, quod illi visa aptior, in qua sensum mysticum fundaret. Sed et in incredulitate et diffidentia, divisioni quidam sensus est, ex qua etiam illi est, ut obstaculo sit divinæ virtuti, dum sic hæsitans non illi firmiter adhæret, sed cogitationibus dividitur.
anchorLine: ἔχει σχολάζουσαν (a). Ὁπηνίκα γοῦν ταύτην λύσει,
en: On 'having the power of thinking and being thought, entirely at leisure.' The editor takes 'vacant, idle' (as already 'above thought') to mean that the mind has the power of the soul by which it thinks of itself or anything else, rather suffering a divine inflowing by which it is already made and becomes god. This is Maximus's plain meaning, expressed in countless places and most familiar to all mystics, as in the phrase 'having become above the being of things, to receive the illumination of the divine and unconquerable monad', as in ch. 95 of the preceding Century. Picus, in the opposite sense, 'strives with all his strength to understand and to be understood', which would be 'busy' (ascholazousan), and is quite alien; Picus's mind has not advanced far enough for the mystics' silence, leisure and darkness, and is busy with natural contemplation without rising spiritually to God. The editor adds that Maximus's explanation here and in ch. 11 of 'diakrithe' as 'were divided' departs from the common one: the Vulgate and Erasmus render 'kai me diakrithe' 'and shall not doubt', which the following 'but shall believe' (faith of miracles, opposed to hesitation and distrust) suggested, and Suidas glosses 'diakrinetai' as 'is in doubt, disbelieves'; but the first sense (divided) pleased Maximus more, since it was apter to ground a mystic sense, though there is a kind of division in unbelief and distrust too, whereby it becomes an obstacle to divine power, since the doubter does not cling firmly but is divided by thoughts.

anchorLine: ἀπὸ τοῦ νεκρῶσαι (b) τῇ καθ' ἁμαρτίαν ἀργίᾳ τὰ
en: On 'from the deadening.' The editor says that whatever Picus offers here is so alien to theology and to knowledge of the movement (of the soul) that this one case could serve as an example that the sacred inner shrines are not easily entered by one who is uninitiated (amyetos). For what has 'sluggishness of sin' and the other things he adds here to do with it? Maximus's own words are clear. The note comments on Picus's rendering; it neither supplies nor deletes a word.
